title: Welcome
hookLine: the parish door should be wide
tomorrow: tree up now, or wait for Christmas Eve? who's right?

cards: Sunday, a few minutes into Mass, the back door creaks. Someone slips in late, doesn't know when to stand, holds the songbook upside down. Hardly anyone turns around.
Matthew's Gospel says who that might be. In Jesus's picture of the last judgment, the king says, in the Douay-Rheims Bible: "I was a stranger, and you took me in." And here's the odd part.
The people he's praising have no idea what he's talking about.

teach.h: WHEN DID WE SEE THEE A STRANGER?
teach.b: They ask him: "And when did we see thee a stranger, and took thee in?" They don't remember it. And the ones he sends away are just as confused: when did we see you a stranger and not help?

Nobody in the scene knew. That's the puzzle, and it's also the answer. If the welcome only counted when you knew it was Jesus at the door, you'd welcome carefully, saving it for the guests who seem important.
The parable takes that option away. As long as you did it to one of these my least brethren, the king says, you did it to me. So the door has to be wide for everyone, because you never know.
Here's something to tell a friend tonight: the command to welcome the stranger is older than the Gospels.
In Leviticus, the Torah tells Israel to treat the stranger living among them like one born in the land, and to love him as themselves, because they were strangers in Egypt.
Jews read that line, Catholics read it, and Jesus stands on it here.
Pope Francis put it this way: the Church is the Father's house with open doors, not a tollhouse. In a parish, that looks small.
A nod. A seat saved. Showing the late guy which page, without a look that says he should have been on time.

how: Catholic parishes welcome newcomers through greeters at the doors, hospitality after Mass and invitations to parish life; Matthew 25 and the Church's teaching on welcoming the stranger stand behind it.

o: the polite smile you give visitors
opening the door before you know who's there
a greeting card sent to new neighbors

games.q: the stranger in Matthew 25 — tap the pairs.
p: I was a stranger, and you took me in
when did we see thee a stranger?

s: the people the king praises knew they were welcoming Jesus
they're surprised: when did we see thee a stranger?
the Torah also commands welcoming the stranger
Leviticus tells Israel to love the stranger, for they were strangers in Egypt.
this parable is about being kind to fellow believers
the king says the least of these. nobody checked who was at the door.

games.q: you're greeting at the door when a family shows up late, kids loud, clearly new. Mass has started. what does Matthew 25 point you to?
o: quietly find them seats and show them the page.
point them to the back so nobody gets distracted.
wait to see if they come back next week first.
games.why: the people the king praises just took the stranger in, without checking first. the door is wide.

practice: Bring to mind one person who's new somewhere you are: a new kid on the team, a coworker in their first month, a family that just moved in.
Write them a short message, the kind you'd want in their spot, something like glad you're here. Send it or keep it as a version, and hold their name for the rest of the sit.

wordCard.voice: Welcome. Opening the door before you know who's there, because in Matthew, nobody knew.

orig.note: Greek, from Matthew 25: I was a stranger and you took me in.

carryVoice: Keep this: the door is wide. Nobody in Matthew checked who was knocking before they opened up.
